scenes.text: A 284B model, 64 GB of RAM, no GPU. Where do the weights that don't fit go?
scenes.say: A two hundred and eighty-four billion parameter model. Sixty-four gigabytes of RAM. No graphics card. So where do the weights that don't fit go?

scenes.headline: How a 284B MoE fits in 64 GB of RAM
scenes.sub: llama-modchip, checked byte by byte against its own files
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Bexley! I expected a trick with the disk. There isn't one. Let's count the bytes.

scenes.title: Two different sizes
scenes.sub: What a model holds, and what a token reads

steps.term: Mixture of experts: many blocks, few used
steps.say: DeepSeek V4 Flash has forty-three layers. In each, a router scores two hundred and fifty-six experts for every token.
Only the top six run. The other two hundred and fifty stay idle, but any of them could be picked next token.
A shared expert runs for everyone, and attention runs every time too.

steps.note: total parameters set capacity; active ones set bandwidth
steps.say: So the whole model has to fit in memory. But a token only reads a small slice of it. Those are two different numbers.

scenes.title: The file fits; a token reads a slice

steps.term: GGUF header: every tensor's name, type and offset
steps.say: I parsed the header of the default checkpoint. Fifty-six point nine three gibibytes, and routed experts are ninety-two point seven percent of it.
One token reads six of two hundred and fifty-six slices per layer. That is one point three three gigabytes: a quarter of its reads.
Attention is a few percent of the file, yet every token reads all of it: two point five four gigabytes.
Add the shared expert and the output head, and one token pulls five point three six gigabytes through the memory bus.

scenes.title: From bytes to a speed limit

steps.say: Start with the bytes: five point three six gigabytes per token.

steps.term: Bandwidth: bytes the bus moves per second
steps.say: The README's desktop sustains about seventy-five gigabytes a second.
Divide, and a token can't take less than seventy-one and a half milliseconds.
That caps decoding at fourteen tokens a second.
The README measures eight point seven five. Sixty-two percent of the ceiling, which is where tuned CPU inference usually lands.

scenes.title: Why not stream it?
scenes.sub: The disk is slower than the bits are worth
scenes.say: Chapter two. Why not stream the experts from disk?

scenes.title: Two ways to hold 277B expert weights

left.title: Map the file, stream experts
left.say: The obvious design maps the file and reads experts from an SSD on demand. At about seven gigabytes a second, with nothing cached, that is four point one tokens a second.

right.title: Squeeze experts until they fit
right.say: This project does the opposite. Most expert weights go to a stock llama.cpp format at about one and a half bits, and the whole file stays in RAM.

scenes.title: Three weights, seven bits
scenes.sub: The vector quantizer behind the repo's name
scenes.say: Chapter three. Three weights, seven bits.

params.cb: the shipped codebook: 128 entries, 7 bits per triple
params.lookup: VPERMI2B looks up 64 bytes in one instruction

steps.say: A three bit scalar quantizer gives each weight eight levels. Three weights then sit on a grid of five hundred and twelve points, evenly through a cube.

steps.term: Codebook: a table of points to snap to
steps.say: Vector quantization snaps the triple as a unit, to a codebook of a hundred and twenty-eight points. That costs seven bits per three weights.
A block holds sixty-four weights: a scale, twenty seven-bit indices, two short tail indices, and eight small sub-scales.
That is a hundred and ninety-two bits, exactly three bits per weight.
The whole codebook fits in six vector registers, so one instruction expands sixty-four bytes of indices without touching memory.

scenes.title: Decoding one weight
scenes.text: w = d x G x m x c[idx]

parts.say: m is the sub-scale for its group of eight,

parts.note: one int8 coordinate of a codebook entry
parts.say: and c is one coordinate of the codebook entry its index names.

steps.say: And here it runs: the Nemotron thirty B build, on a free eight-core cloud instance with thirty-two gigabytes and no GPU.
The status bar shows an eight K context window. Short prompts only: a coding agent's long system prompt did not fit.

scenes.title: What the quality numbers measure
scenes.say: The quality claims need a closer read.

items.say: Ninety-nine point one five percent is one tensor, quantized and restored, from the thirty B model. It says nothing about the big model's answers.
The big model never ran at full precision, so its divergence is measured against its own default build.
And on the thirty B, every variant scores a hundred on the gate. A test everyone aces cannot rank them.

scenes.text: The 284B fits because its experts are squeezed to 1.6 bits; its speed is set by the layers every token reads.
scenes.say: The big model fits because its experts are squeezed to about one point six bits. Its speed is set by the layers every token reads.

recap: 5.36 GB per token, a quarter of it experts
scenes.say: To recap. A token reads five point three six gigabytes, a quarter of it experts. Nothing streams. And vector quantization packs three weights into seven bits.
